paragraphs: I was allowed to do an eight-week clerkship at the Medical University of Gdansk in Poland. There were many firsts and I was anxious about dormitory life, to which I was unaccustomed, but many people supported me both in Japan and on site, and I was able to spend a very meaningful time. Although it is only a part, I would like to introduce what I experienced.

Gdansk is a major port town in Poland facing the Baltic Sea. It is safe and prices are cheap, so it was a very livable place. While rich in nature, transport is also well developed and facilities such as shopping malls are well equipped, so I had no trouble in daily life. We lived in the university dormitory. It is located about a 15-minute walk from the hospital. We were given a single room with basic furniture provided, and there was nothing in particular I had to prepare additionally. The washbasin is in the room, but the kitchen, shower, toilet and washing machine are shared. Many exchange students other than us also lived there, and even within the dormitory we could interact with other students, such as Italians treating us to pasta and, conversely, our making okonomiyaki and eating it together.

The biggest feature of the Medical University of Gdansk is its international character. There are two courses, the Polish Division and the English Division (ED), and the ED has students enrolled from various countries, and there were also very many exchange students sent through ERASMUS, the EU exchange system. Although it is Europe, there were also Indian and Asian students, and I could experience many cultural differences. We took part in the ED clerkships and were able to do the clerkships in English. Because the official language is Polish, there were scenes in outpatient clerkships where the doctor interpreted, but young patients can speak English, so there were also opportunities to take histories directly. As for the clerkship system, as at Nagoya University, in the fourth and fifth years students are divided into small groups and rotate every one week to one month to do clerkships in all departments, and then in the sixth year they seem to choose several departments and do clerkships fixed for a longer period. I rotated through five: obstetrics and gynecology, pediatrics, pediatric surgery, urology and Family Medicine. In every subject there was a test on the last day. The format was multiple choice or an oral examination, and in the oral examination, rather than one-question-one-answer, knowledge was confirmed through discussion between the group members and the doctor using a case, with an atmosphere like PBL, which was fresh. There were also many lectures, and a lecture on obesity was treated as important, in which I felt a difference from Japan. In pediatrics I took histories from guardians and actually did physical examinations, and in urology I performed cystoscopy examinations on patients, so I was able to do things I could not experience in clerkships in Japan.

On site I was especially greatly supported by Professor Wozniak of biochemistry and the attending student Pawel. The professor welcomed us warmly like family. On the day we arrived, although it was the middle of the night, he came to pick us up at the airport, and brought daily necessities and food to the dormitory for us. On holidays we ate together and went hanami (cherry blossom viewing), and he was always concerned about whether we were doing well. Pawel also invited us to his home and held a party, creating a place where we could interact with local students, and when I fell ill he bought medicine and rushed to the dormitory. In addition, at an event called Nagoya Day hosted by the professor, we gave a presentation on tea to local students and held a discussion about school life.

Taking part in this program had been a goal since before I entered university, so I am simply happy that I could take part. Living in an unfamiliar place was full of anxiety, but many people held out a helping hand, and it was a period in which I learned and grew in many ways, not only academically but as a person. In particular, I was greatly helped by the generosity with which everyone I met there accepted new people and by their attitude of actively engaging with them. It has now been several months since I returned to Japan, and I can feel that my own behavior has changed compared with before the study abroad. Finally, I thank everyone who was involved in this study abroad. Thank you very much.
